clue.text: Cigarette famine locally ?

parts.note: an area where, by law, nothing may be burnt to give off fumes reads as a district with no cigarettes

explanation.surface: A local shortage of cigarettes leaves smokers desperate.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue pretends a district has run out of cigarettes; really it describes a British clean-air area where burning coal and other fuels that give off fumes is banned.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain the Clean Air Acts set up districts where only fuels that give off no fumes may be burnt, so in a sense no smoking happens there.

clue.text: A makeshift ditty ?

parts.note: read make-shift as making a shift, a woman's chemise, so the ditty is one about sewing garments

explanation.surface: An improvised little tune.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood's 1843 poem about an exploited seamstress ('Stitch! stitch! stitch!') is a song about making a shift, an undergarment.
explanation.definitionFit: Hood's poem laments a seamstress sewing garments, so it is literally a song about shift-making.

clue.text: Not always sound in the body

definitions.meaning: a church instrument is often silent, so it is not always making music
a part such as the heart or liver inside a living body

explanation.surface: A doctor admits the body is not always healthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' looks like healthy, but here it means making music: the church instrument is silent between services.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a keyboard instrument with pipes and a bodily part like the liver.

clue.text: Former coastal flier on our side outwardly

parts.note: ex- means former
a tern is a seabird of coasts
an ally is on our side

explanation.surface: A former seaside bird watcher speaks of something on our side.
explanation.definitionFit: Externally means on the outside, in outward appearance.

clue.text: Crossbill passed in cathedral city ? Quite so

indicators.note: in shows the two pieces sit inside the city's name

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire
X is the shape of a cross
a bill passed by Parliament becomes an Act

explanation.surface: A crossbill, the finch, flew past in a cathedral city; someone agrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Crossbill' is split: X (a cross) and ACT (a bill that has been passed) go inside ELY, an English cathedral city.
explanation.definitionFit: Exactly is a phrase of agreement meaning precisely so.

clue.text: Is turned on to play an old sacred instrument

indicators.note: in a down clue on means placed above the next piece
turned means the word is is written backwards

parts.note: taken as written
to strum is to play a stringed instrument casually

explanation.surface: Someone is turned on to playing an ancient temple instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: IS turned gives SI, placed on top of STRUM in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The sistrum is an ancient Egyptian rattle used in worship of Isis.

clue.text: Man couchant ?

parts.note: the name reads the same when laid on its side, and adding man gives a word for a couch

explanation.surface: A heraldic man lying down.
explanation.walkthrough: Couchant is heraldic for lying down. This man's name, followed by MAN, makes an ottoman, a couch, and it reads the same either way round.
explanation.definitionFit: Otto is a man's name, and with man appended it gives a backless couch.

clue.text: Put me up to be grilled as being ' implicated

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word me is written bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
to broil is to grill

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be put up for a grilling as a suspect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put me up' turns ME into EM in this down clue; BROILED is the American word for grilled.
explanation.definitionFit: Embroiled means caught up in a conflict or scandal, involved.

clue.text: Perhaps Belloc's favourite version of Lamb

definitions.text: Perhaps Belloc's favourite version of Lamb

parts.words: Perhaps Belloc's favourite version of Lamb
parts.note: Belloc loved the Sussex hills, so his ideal lamb would be the breed named after them

explanation.surface: Wonders which essay by Charles Lamb Hilaire Belloc liked best.
explanation.walkthrough: Lamb looks like the essayist Charles Lamb, but it is the animal. Hilaire Belloc celebrated Sussex and its chalk hills, the South Downs, which give a breed of sheep its name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Southdown is a breed of sheep from the Sussex chalk hills that Belloc praised.

clue.text: Birds--" that go bump …" ?

parts.note: the old prayer asks deliverance from 'things that go bump in the night', and these birds call by night with a churring sound

explanation.surface: A bird quotation trailing off into the old ghostly prayer about things that go bump.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish prayer 'From ghoulies and ghosties ... and things that go bump in the night' is completed by the bird's name split as NIGHT JARS: a jar is a jolt or bump.
explanation.definitionFit: Nightjars are nocturnal birds, and a jar in the night is a bump in the night.

clue.text: Prohibition; a bootlegger makes a false start

indicators.note: a false start means the word begins wrongly, with its closing letter brought round to open it

parts.note: a bootlegger's name begins with the word boot, which is all that is taken here

explanation.surface: A bootlegger in the Prohibition era makes a botched start to his career.
explanation.walkthrough: A BOOT, taken from the opening of 'a bootlegger', is given a false start by moving its final T to the front, giving TABOO. The surface sets Prohibition beside a bootlegger to suggest 1920s America.
explanation.definitionFit: A taboo is a ban or forbidding of something, a social prohibition.

clue.text: Man of property

parts.note: a man who has property is one who holds title to it; also the title of the first Forsyte novel by Galsworthy

explanation.surface: Recalls Galsworthy's novel The Man of Property.
explanation.walkthrough: The Man of Property is the first novel of Galsworthy's Forsyte Saga, but here the phrase is simply read as a person who holds property.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who holds legal title to land or goods is the possessor of property.

clue.text: Lining out changes sides

parts.note: a garment worn with its lining outside has been ... inside out, and a person who does so figuratively switches allegiance

explanation.surface: A garment worn inside out, its lining showing, flips sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The image is a jacket turned inside out so its lining shows; the phrase for that act also names a traitor who changes sides.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat is a traitor or deserter, someone who swaps loyalty, as if reversing a jacket.

clue.text: See 12
Playing over and over

parts.note: a game played in overs, sets of six balls, means playing over after over

explanation.surface: Something played repeatedly.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, the bat-and-ball game, play is divided into overs of six balls, so playing it is playing over after over.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket is played in overs, so taking part in it is playing over upon over.

clue.text: One way to get a bird from a bush

definitions.text: One way to get a bird from a bush

parts.words: One way to get a bird from a bush
parts.note: clipping a hedge into the shape of a peacock or other animal makes a bird out of a shrub

explanation.surface: Echoes the proverb about a bird in the hand being worth two in the bush.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush' suggests catching one; instead the gardener clips the bush itself into a bird shape.
explanation.definitionFit: Topiary is the art of clipping shrubs into ornamental shapes such as peacocks.

clue.text: Horses in stalls ? No, their lot is inferior

definitions.text: Horses in stalls ? No, their lot is inferior

parts.words: Horses in stalls ? No, their lot is inferior
parts.note: in a theatre the cheap ground floor area lies below the stalls, and these horses worked underground in coal mines

explanation.surface: Asks whether stabled horses have a good life, then says their fate is poor.
explanation.walkthrough: Stalls suggests horses in stables or theatre stalls; the pit is a cheaper theatre area and also a coal mine, where ponies hauled coal underground: their lot was literally lower.
explanation.definitionFit: Pit ponies were small horses that hauled coal tubs underground in mines.

clue.text: Elgin type of red lamb ?

indicators.note: the answer is made out of the letters, read as formed of the words that follow in a new order

explanation.surface: Asks what kind of meat a red lamb might be, as if a cut from Elgin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Elgin Marbles are the Parthenon sculptures in the British Museum; the answer, an anagram of RED LAMB, describes their kind of stone-patterned look. 'Type' belongs to the definition, 'of' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Something streaked like marble resembles the stone of the Elgin Marbles, the Greek sculptures in the British Museum.

clue.text: Star who married the Dickensian Spider

definitions.meaning: the girl's name comes from Latin stella, a star
in Great Expectations Pip's beloved marries Bentley Drummle, whom Jaggers nicknames the Spider

explanation.surface: A celebrity wedding to a creepy character from Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Great Expectations Jaggers calls the brutish Bentley Drummle 'the Spider', and Miss Havisham's ward weds him.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine's name derives from the Latin word for a celestial body, and she is the Great Expectations ward who weds Drummle.

clue.text: Recklessness of the political wagon?

parts.note: a word for recklessness splits to describe musicians riding on the wagon that politicians jump on

explanation.surface: Asks about the recklessness of the political bandwagon.
explanation.walkthrough: Politicians jump on the bandwagon; split as A BAND ON, the word for wild recklessness describes the musicians aboard.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandon is unrestrained freedom of manner, careless wildness.

clue.text: Thieving fellow returning stack of notes talks with the beak

definitions.note: a noun sense is meant: a bird that can mimic speech, using its bill

parts.note: Jack is a stock name for any man or fellow

indicators.note: returning means the word for a bundle of banknotes is read backwards

parts.note: a wad is a thick bundle of banknotes

explanation.surface: A thieving man counts a roll of notes and chats with a magistrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beak' looks like British slang for a magistrate, but here it is the bird's bill: this crow is known for stealing shiny things and can be taught to speak. 'Thieving' adds colour to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The jackdaw, a small crow, is famous for pilfering bright objects and for mimicking human words.

clue.text: A celebrated occasion

parts.note: celebrated means both famous and marked by festivities, as an anniversary of a reign

explanation.surface: A famous event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Celebrated' looks like famous, but it means marked with festivities, as an anniversary of a monarch's reign is.
explanation.definitionFit: A jubilee is a special anniversary, such as of a reign, marked with festivities.

clue.text: A Victorian miss played with it before she wore it

definitions.text: A Victorian miss played with it before she wore it

parts.words: A Victorian miss played with it before she wore it
parts.note: a girl bowled a ring along with a stick as a child, then wore a ring-framed skirt as a young woman

explanation.surface: A Victorian girl's toy later becomes part of her wardrobe.
explanation.walkthrough: Victorian children bowled a wooden ring with a stick; grown women wore crinolines held out by rings of whalebone or steel.
explanation.definitionFit: The same ring served as a child's bowling toy and as the stiffening frame of a crinoline skirt.

clue.text: Blame this should the door stick ? Maybe

definitions.text: Blame this should the door stick ? Maybe

parts.words: Blame this should the door stick ? Maybe
parts.note: the upright side post of a door frame is the part to fault when a door jams

explanation.surface: A homeowner looks for something to blame when the door gets stuck.
explanation.walkthrough: The side post of a door frame sounds like jam, to stick, so it is the natural culprit when a door sticks.
explanation.definitionFit: A jamb is the vertical side post of a doorway or window frame.

clue.text: Could be real, Bob — property of a lord

indicators.note: could be says the letters might make another word if rearranged

parts.note: bob was slang for a shilling, abbreviated s in old British money

explanation.surface: A man wonders if a shilling coin is genuine, then mentions a lord's estate.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange REAL to EARL and add S, from 'Bob', slang for a shilling (s.) in pre-decimal British money. The definition is possessive: belonging to a peer.
explanation.definitionFit: A peer of this rank owns the property, so the possessive form means belonging to a nobleman.

clue.text: Music a chaperon doubtless comprehends

indicators.note: comprehends means contains, so the piece is held within the letters of the following words

explanation.surface: A chaperon surely understands music.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is held across 'chapeRON DOubtless'; 'comprehends' looks like understands but means contains.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form in which a main theme returns between episodes.

clue.text: The good of being beaten ?

definitions.meaning: wellbeing or prosperity, as in the common good
a raised mark left on skin by a lash

explanation.surface: Asks what good comes of a beating.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both welfare, as in commonweal, and a raised ridge on skin left by a whip.

clue.text: How to get money to build

definitions.meaning: to collect funds, as in gathering capital
to put up or erect a structure

explanation.surface: A developer's two steps: find the cash, then construct.
explanation.definitionFit: One verb covers both collecting funds, as in a loan or tax, and erecting a building.

clue.text: All one gets in the dance is flirtation

indicators.note: in shows the first pieces are placed inside the word for the dance

parts.note: taken as written, the word dance
taken as written
one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Everyone at the ball is flirting.
explanation.walkthrough: ALL plus I (one, in Roman numerals) go inside DANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Dalliance is light amorous play, a casual romance without commitment.

clue.text: A shivering few leaving a party

parts.note: to shiver can mean to break into fragments, so a shivering is a splinter
a few people form a small group

explanation.surface: A few people, cold and shivering, slip away from a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shivering' looks like trembling from cold, but to shiver is also to shatter into slivers. The definition describes a faction that breaks away from a political party.
explanation.definitionFit: A faction that breaks away from its parent political body is a breakaway faction.
